Title: Blood transfusion in preterm infants improves intestinal tissue oxygenation without alteration in blood flow.

Journal/Date: Vox sanguinis (2016)

MeSH Keywords: Blood Flow Velocity, Blood Transfusion, Female, Humans, Infant, Infant, Newborn, Infant, Premature, Male


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE]: The objective of the study was to investigate the splanchnic blood flow velocity and oximetry response to blood transfusion in preterm infants according to postnatal age.
[MATERIALS AND METHODS]: Preterm infants receiving blood transfusion were recruited to three groups: 1-7 (group 1; n = 20), 8-28 (group 2; n = 21) and ≥29 days of life (group 3; n = 18). Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) peak systolic (PSV) and diastolic velocities were measured 30-60 min pre- and post-transfusion using Doppler ultrasound scan. Splanchnic tissue haemoglobin index (sTHI), tissue oxygenation index (sTOI) and fractional tissue oxygen extraction (sFTOE) were measured from 15-20 min before to post-transfusion using near-infrared spectroscopy.
[RESULTS]: The mean pretransfusion Hb in group 1, 2 and 3 was 11, 10 and 9 g/dl, respectively. The mean (SD) pretransfusion SMA PSV in group 1, 2 and 3 was 0·63 (0·32), 0·81 (0·33) and 0·97 (0·40) m/s, respectively, and this did not change significantly following transfusion. The mean (SD) pretransfusion sTOI in group 1, 2 and 3 was 36·7 (19·3), 44·6 (10·4) and 41·3 (10·4)%, respectively. The sTHI and sTOI increased (P < 0·01), and sFTOE decreased (P < 0·01) following transfusion in all groups. On multivariate analysis, changes in SMA PSV and sTOI following blood transfusion were not associated with PDA, feeding, pretransfusion Hb and mean blood pressure.
[CONCLUSION]: Pretransfusion baseline splanchnic tissue oximetry and blood flow velocity varied with postnatal age. Blood transfusion improved intestinal tissue oxygenation without altering mesenteric blood flow velocity irrespective of postnatal ages.

key_findings.finding: Two direct prospective human studies support the proposition that RBC transfusion improves intestinal/splanchnic oxygenation without changing measured mesenteric flow velocity. In PMID 26643925, 20 extremely preterm infants (median GA 26 weeks; first week of life) received transfusion; SMA peak systolic and diastolic velocities were unchanged (p=0.63 and p=0.65), while splanchnic THI increased 32.3% (p<0.01), sTOI increased 14.6% (p=0.03), and sFTOE decreased 22.1% (p<0.01). The authors concluded that transfusion increased intestinal tissue oxygenation but did not alter blood-flow velocities; partial feeding did not modify responses.

key_findings.finding: A second direct prospective study (PMID 27509230; Vox Sanguinis 2016) enrolled 59 preterm infants in three postnatal-age groups (1–7 days n=20, 8–28 days n=21, ≥29 days n=18). Doppler SMA PSV and diastolic velocity were measured 30–60 minutes before/after transfusion, and sTHI, sTOI, and sFTOE by NIRS from 15–20 minutes before through after transfusion. SMA PSV did not change significantly, whereas sTHI and sTOI increased (both p<0.01) and sFTOE decreased (p<0.01) in all age groups. The authors concluded that transfusion improved intestinal tissue oxygenation without altering mesenteric blood-flow velocity, regardless of postnatal age; changes were not explained by PDA, feeding, pretransfusion hemoglobin, or mean blood pressure.

key_findings.finding: Evidence is not uniformly consistent: a prospective cohort of 25 stable infants <32 weeks GA, <1500 g (median GA 26.9 weeks) receiving 15 mL/kg PRBC over 4 hours measured splanchnic NIRS during feeding epochs and Doppler flow. The study's abstract reports that PRBCT was associated with decreased celiac artery flow and failure of the postprandial SMA-flow increase, while NIRS analysis showed increased postprandial splanchnic FTOE during the first post-transfusion epoch (10.55% to 13.21%, p=0.046), interpreted by the authors as possible gut ischemia/transfusion-associated NEC risk. This study therefore does not support a simple universal claim of unchanged flow, and its NIRS endpoint was oxygen extraction/oxygen-utilization efficiency rather than a direct transfusion-induced rise in splanchnic saturation.
